transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 mins
Attendees: Sam Parker (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (BrightBridge Head of ML), Priya Patel (BrightBridge Eng Mgr), Liam O'Connor (BrightBridge Infra)

[00:00] Sam Parker: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — optimize walkthrough, quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), show the console, and then talk about POC next steps.
[00:10] Tom Reyes: Great, excited. We want to reduce inference cost but can't accept big quality regressions. Our baseline is 8-bit quantized Llama-variant running on A100s.
[00:22] Maya Singh: Cool. Quick clarifier — when you say 8-bit baseline, you mean per-tensor INT8 or dynamic per-channel?
[00:28] Tom Reyes: Uh, it's our current stack, it's a vendor pipeline, per-channel, but it's not optimized. We see occasional hallucinations when prompt length grows.
[00:36] Priya Patel: Also our SLO is 100ms p95 for short completions, and most sessions are 30-80 tokens.
[00:44] Maya Singh: OK noted, that's actually pretty tight. We'll demonstrate a couple of profiles that trade a few percent of quality for a 30-50% latency win.
[00:55] Liam O'Connor: Do you support FP8? We heard FP8 on newer kernels has better perf but worry about stability.
[01:02] Sam Parker: Yes, FP8 is supported on our latest runtime on supported GPUs. FP8 can give you middle ground — lower quant noise than naive INT8 with good kernel speedups, depends on model architecture.
[01:15] Maya Singh: I'm going to share my screen — Optimize dashboard — and we'll load the quantization comparison we ran against a Llama-variant with BrightBridge-ish prompts.
[01:30] [screen share noise, rustle]
[01:35] Maya Singh: Okay on screen: left panel is profiles list, we have 'legacy-int8', 'optimize-int8-aggressive', 'fp8-balanced', and 'fp8-safe'. The table shows p50/p95 latency and 'quality score' — that's BLEU-ish + embedding similarity weighted metric we use for internal comparisons. It's imperfect but consistent for rollouts.
[02:05] Tom Reyes: Is that embedding sim on a validation set or live traffic?
[02:09] Maya Singh: Validation set from the benchmark suite — the one we'd like you to send a sample of. Column shows relative quality change vs baseline float16. Note that small deltas under 1.5% are often noise.
[02:24] [02:30] Priya Patel: So what are realistic deltas? If we pick 'optimize-int8-aggressive' what kind of drop?
[02:36] Maya Singh: In this run, aggressive INT8 gave ~1.8% drop on the quality metric, but latency improved by ~48% p95. FP8-balanced had ~0.6% drop and ~35% latency improvement.
[02:50] Tom Reyes: Hmm, 1.8% feels risky on some of our legal summarization prompts — high precision required.
[02:58] Maya Singh: Totally — that's why Optimize supports canary rollouts and per-route profiles. You can route high-sensitivity flows to FP8-safe or to float16 on Dedicated.
[03:10] Sam Parker: Quick note on kernels and hardware — FP8 performance depends on driver and kernel path; A100 and Blackwell support optimized kernels but older gen has limited speedups. We'll run POC on your target infra.
[03:24] Liam O'Connor: Our infra is a mix — some A100, some H100-ish; we can provision for a benchmark.
[03:30] Maya Singh: Great. Another caveat — larger sequence lengths amplify quant errors because KV-cache accumulates small errors. Our config suggests being conservative with INT8 for long context workloads.
[03:45] Tom Reyes: Our average is 60 tokens but we have spikes to 400.
[03:50] Maya Singh: For spikes, two options: use adaptive profile that switches to FP8 or float16 past token threshold, or keep a small fraction of requests routed to float16 as a safety net.
[04:02] [04:10] Sam Parker: I'll jump to the Optimize 'rollouts' tab — shows canary percentages, auto rollback conditions (quality delta threshold, error rate increase, latency SLA breach).
[04:25] Priya Patel: Can the rollback trigger use a custom metric from our evals?
[04:29] Maya Singh: Yes, you can push custom regression metrics via the SDK or webhook. We also ingest model outputs and run prompt-level checks if you enable the evals add-on.
[04:40] Tom Reyes: You mentioned automatic prefix/KV caching earlier — does that interact with quant profiles?
[04:45] Maya Singh: It does. Caching avoids repeated token compute and can reduce noise because the cached kv is stored in full precision in our cache by default. That means subsequent tokens after a cached prefix see less compounding quant error.
[04:58] Liam O'Connor: Storage overhead?
[05:00] Maya Singh: Cache size is configurable; we balance memory vs latency. For BrightBridge load patterns, caching warm prefixes gave us a 12-20% latency improvement in tests.
[05:12] [05:20] Tom Reyes: Let's talk numbers — can we replicate your results?
[05:23] Maya Singh: Absolutely. For the POC we propose: 2-days, we run the same prompt set through three profiles: baseline float16, fp8-balanced, optimize-int8-aggressive. We'll produce per-prompt quality diff, p50/p95 latency, token cost, and fairness tests.
[05:40] Priya Patel: Fairness tests?
[05:42] Maya Singh: Basic distributional checks — answer length, hallucination markers, and a few custom checks you define.
[05:49] Tom Reyes: How do you measure hallucinations automatically? It's tricky.
[05:52] Maya Singh: We use a combination of entailment checks and semantic similarity to reference answers where available. It's not perfect but good enough to flag regressions that need human review.
[06:06] [06:15] Priya Patel: On the infra side, if we run this on Dedicated GPUs, will costs be estimated in the report?
[06:20] Sam Parker: Yes — Optimize will estimate token-level cost based on throughput and reserved capacity assumptions. We'll also provide a recommendation if Dedicated is required to meet your SLOs.
[06:30] Tom Reyes: About FP8 — do we need to change model weights or does Redwood do on-the-fly quantization?
[06:37] Maya Singh: We do profile-guided quantization on-the-fly in the serving path — no manual weight conversion required. For aggressive profiles we do a one-time per-commit calibration step but it's automated.
[06:49] Liam O'Connor: Any security concerns with calibration data leaving our cluster?
[06:52] Sam Parker: For Dedicated/Private deployments, calibration and profiling can run entirely inside your VPC — nothing leaves your network unless you opt in.
[07:02] Tom Reyes: Good.
[07:05] [07:10] Maya Singh: I'm going to pull up a sample per-prompt report — here's prompt #23, float16 answer vs fp8 vs int8. You can see the fp8 answer preserves key entities better than the int8 one where a date got swapped.
[07:25] Tom Reyes: Yeah that's the kind of failure we need to catch. Can we mark that prompt as 'sensitive' and always route float16?
[07:31] Maya Singh: Yep — per-route overrides are supported. We'll demo setting that in the console.
[07:40] [07:50] Maya Singh: Quick demo — create new rollout: select model family, create 'fp8-safe' profile, set canary 5% for 24h, add monitors: quality_delta > 1% for flagged prompts, error_rate > 0.5%, latency p95 > 120ms. Then hit start.
[08:10] Priya Patel: When monitoring quality_delta, can we restrict to a prompt set?
[08:14] Maya Singh: Yes, you can upload a validation set or attach a tag to routes. The alerting engine accepts that.
[08:20] [08:30] Tom Reyes: What's the overhead of FP8 in throughput terms vs float16?
[08:32] Maya Singh: In our bench: FP8 gave ~1.6x token throughput over float16 on Blackwell-like hardware; INT8 aggressive was ~2x but with higher variance in quality. On A100 numbers are a little lower but still material.
[08:47] Sam Parker: Also note batching plays a role. We can do continuous batching which helps throughput while keeping latency under your SLO by prioritizing short requests.
[08:59] Liam O'Connor: Any prepackaged configs you recommend for summarization vs chat vs embeddings?
[09:04] Maya Singh: Yes — Optimize has template profiles: chat-short, chat-long, summarization-safe. We can start you on summarization-safe for your legal flows.
[09:12] Tom Reyes: Can we drive these via API or only Console?
[09:15] Maya Singh: Both — everything in the Console is backed by API. We'll include example SDK calls in the follow-up.
[09:23] [09:30] Priya Patel: For the POC, what's required from our side?
[09:33] Maya Singh: Representative prompt set (ideally 500-1,000 prompts), one week of anonymized traces if possible, target GPU spec for running the bench (we can also run in our hosted env), and an agreed list of regression checks.
[09:45] Tom Reyes: We can get 500 prompts and a 1k trace.
[09:48] Sam Parker: Perfect. We'll produce a schedule and a data handoff doc after this call.
[09:55] [10:00] Maya Singh: Any other technical questions?
[10:02] Tom Reyes: One more — how do you handle model rollbacks on in-flight requests if a rollback triggers?
[10:07] Maya Singh: We do gradual draining. New requests go to the fallback profile while in-flight tokens finish with the previous one. We avoid mid-request model swaps to reduce inconsistencies.
[10:20] Liam O'Connor: OK makes sense.
[10:25] Sam Parker: I'll recap next steps near the end but quick Q — competitor question, have you evaluated Hugging Face hosted endpoints or Triton at all?
[10:34] Tom Reyes: We played with Hugging Face but ran into cost surprises, and Triton is in infra experiments but no production yet.
[10:41] Sam Parker: Good to know.
[10:45] [10:50] Maya Singh: Skipping ahead to the cost table — Optimize outputs estimated per-token cost, factoring in batching, KV cache hit rates, and reserved capacity. For BrightBridge load our model, fp8-balanced lowered the per-token cost by ~28% vs float16 in our sample run. INT8 aggressive about ~45%.
[11:10] Tom Reyes: That's compelling but need to balance those cases where accuracy matters.
[11:14] Priya Patel: How long does calibration take?
[11:17] Maya Singh: Usually minutes to an hour depending on model size and samples. The system parallelizes calibration across GPUs.
[11:24] Tom Reyes: Anything else about observability?
[11:27] Maya Singh: Console has per-route traces, token-level timing breakdowns, and drift detection charts. We'll enable RBAC so only certain users can change profiles.
[11:38] Sam Parker: Security stuff — we'll share SOC2 and Private deployment docs. For Dedicated, audit logs and KMS integration are standard.
[11:47] Tom Reyes: Great.
[11:50] [11:55] Sam Parker: Alright let's recap and assign actions.
[12:00] Sam Parker: Next steps — Sam sends pricing and POC plan, Maya sends quant spreadsheet and config, Tom and team provide prompts and traces. We'll schedule the POC for next week if timelines align.
[12:15] Tom Reyes: Sounds good. Thanks both.
[12:20] Priya Patel: Thank you.
[12:23] Maya Singh: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[12:27] Sam Parker: Bye.

End of transcript.
